# On accepting a drink from a stranger: a note on Han Seo-yeon's "Small Courtesies"

The passage comes from Han Seo-yeon's etiquette column in a Seoul weekly. It answers a reader who sat alone at a bar, was offered a drink by a man she did not know, and froze between two rules she had been given:

> "The rule against taking things from strangers is a rule for children walking home from school. An adult at a bar who refuses a drink outright tells the other person he has been judged a danger. Accept it, thank him, and you owe him nothing more than conversation for as long as the glass lasts. That is what the gesture means here, and to pretend otherwise turns a small kindness into an accusation."
>
> (Han Seo-yeon, "Small Courtesies")

Han makes three claims. First, a rule learned in childhood has been applied to a situation it was never made for. Second, refusing communicates suspicion, and that suspicion wounds. Third, what the gift asks in return is small and bounded: a thank-you and some conversation, and nothing beyond that.

I agree with much of this, and I will say where. I also have to correct something I wrote earlier. The first version of this note was wrong in a way a reader caught, and the correction changes what I think the right answer is.

**Where I agree with Han.** Giving gifts and receiving hospitality are found in every society we know of, and stinginess and coldness are disapproved of nearly everywhere. A small gift between strangers is one of the oldest ways people test whether they can be at ease with each other. Han is right that suspicion has a cost. Suppose everyone treated every unasked-for kindness as a probable threat. Strangers could hardly meet. Every friendly gesture would carry the risk of being taken as an insult, so fewer people would make one, and a bar would become a room of people sitting carefully apart. A habit like that leaves almost everyone worse off and protects few. So the childhood rule, carried unchanged into adult life, is not a virtue.

Her third claim seems to me the wisest. A gift that obliges the receiver to more than thanks and a little company has become a purchase. By putting a firm, small limit on the debt, she protects the receiver more than a rule of refusal would. The person who accepts knows exactly what she has agreed to, and anyone who expects more is the one breaking the custom.

**Where I went wrong.** In my first draft I went beyond Han. I wrote that the virtuous habit was ready acceptance, a willingness to take the offered glass with good grace. I tested that habit by asking what would happen if everyone at the bar held it. I imagined the buyer who means well, the receiver who takes the drink, and the room that becomes warmer for it. The test seemed to pass, and I said so.

A reader named Bae Jung-ah wrote to me afterwards. She has tended bar near Sinchon for nine years. Her objection was short. I had tested the habit from the buyer's position and from the room's, but not from the position of a person sitting alone when the buyer is not what he appears to be. She also told me something I did not know: in her bar, and in many like it, the custom already has a settled form. The offer goes through the bartender. She pours the drink in front of the person, or carries it over and says who sent it. If the person does not want it, she can decline to the bartender, who passes on her thanks, and nothing is said to the man's face. "Your version teaches people to take the glass from his hand," Bae wrote. "Mine costs him nothing."

She was right, and I want to be exact about why, because my error was in the test itself and not only in my conclusion.

A habit counts as a virtue only if it stays stable once most people hold it, meaning no one gains by dropping it or by exploiting it. "Accept the drink a stranger hands you" fails that standard. The more people hold it, the more it rewards the rare man who means harm, because he can count on the glass being taken. The habit pays the exploiter precisely to the extent that it spreads. That is the shape of a vice's opportunity. I missed it because I asked whether the habit made the room pleasant, when I should have asked whether it made the room safe for the person with the least protection in it. I should have judged without knowing which seat would be mine, and I did not do that carefully enough.

Bae's form passes where mine failed. Under the bartender-routed custom, the honest buyer loses nothing. His gesture arrives, his name is given, and his kindness is acknowledged. The receiver keeps every part of the courtesy Han values. She can accept warmly, raise the glass to him across the room, and talk with him as long as she likes. But the dishonest buyer gains nothing he could not have had by sitting quietly, because the drink never passes through his hands. Under this arrangement nobody does better by abandoning the custom, which is what makes it a virtue and not merely a pleasantry. The courtesy and the caution are not in tension here. The custom holds both.

I have rewritten my answer to Han's reader to say this. If she would like the drink, she should accept it from the bartender's hand, or watch it poured. If the man offers to carry it to her himself, she can say, without accusing him of anything, that she would rather order it from the bar, and he can buy it there. If he takes offence at that, the offence tells her something.

**Where I still differ from Han.** One point remains open between her column and my reading of it. Han says that refusing outright tells the buyer he has been judged a danger. Sometimes it does. More often, I think, it tells him only that the person does not want a drink, or does not want company tonight, or does not drink, or came to the bar specifically to sit alone. A plain "thank you, I'm fine," said with a smile, is a courtesy of its own. It answers a gift with thanks, which is all Han herself says the gift requires. If refusal is always read as an insult, then accepting becomes compulsory, and a gift that cannot be declined is no longer quite a gift. Han's own rule about the bounded debt seems to me to imply this, though she does not say it.

I put this to Bae as well. She partly agreed. In her experience, she said, most men take a refusal relayed by the bartender well and take one given to their face less well, which is part of why the custom routes it through her. That is a point about how people actually behave, and it carries more weight than my reasoning about what refusal ought to mean. I accept it for bars that have such a custom. Many places do not have one: a counter seat at a small izakaya, a crowded pojangmacha with one person cooking and serving at once. There the person alone may have to choose between the glass in a stranger's hand and saying no to him directly. I do not yet have a good answer for those rooms. I have asked Bae what she would do in one, and she has not written back.

**Household AI tutors in Kenyan junior secondary schooling: a case study**

*From* Learning at Home: Technology and the Competency-Based Curriculum in East Africa, *chapter 7, "Assistants in the household"*

**7.4 The Langat household, Eldoret (2025–2026)**

This case comes from a two-year study of eleven households in Uasin Gishu County. Each household used an openly licensed AI assistant called Musonius on a shared family phone and on a school tablet. The families agreed to have their logs anonymised and reviewed. Names here are changed.

Kiprono Langat was fifteen and in Grade 9 at a mixed day school on the edge of Eldoret town. He used the assistant almost every evening between about 7 and 9 p.m. His father, Mr. Cheruiyot Langat, is a clerk at the county lands office, and he used the same phone account on weekends, mostly for letters and for questions about the CBC assessment calendar. Kiprono's mother works nights at the referral hospital and rarely appeared in the logs.

Most of the logs are ordinary schoolwork. Across the eighteen months reviewed, about 70 per cent of Kiprono's sessions were integrated science and pre-technical studies. Most of the rest were Kiswahili composition. He tended to write an *insha* in English first, ask the assistant why his translation sounded stiff, and then rewrite it himself. The assistant's replies were short. A typical exchange from March 2025:

> **Kiprono:** is "alikuwa akienda" wrong here
> **Musonius:** Not wrong. "Alikwenda" is enough. You've already said "kila siku," so the habit is clear.

The researchers coded an exchange as a "full answer" when the assistant supplied finished work that Kiprono had not written. Over the eighteen months, such answers made up under 4 per cent of exchanges. Most of them were definitions. He sometimes asked outright for a finished practical report. When he did, the assistant usually asked whether he wanted the report or wanted to be able to write one. Kiprono picked the second option more often than the researchers expected, especially as assessments got closer.

Two other patterns appear in the logs. First, Kiprono often used the assistant to rehearse things he planned to say to adults: a request to his Scouts patrol leader to change camp dates, and an apology to a neighbour after a broken window. Second, he mentioned friends by name, and one of them comes up repeatedly. Nasieku was fourteen, in his class, and from a family that had moved from Kajiado two years before. Over several months she appears in passing: they studied together, she was better at mathematics, and once he wanted help explaining simultaneous equations "the way Nasieku does it."

**The October exchange**

In October 2025 Kiprono started a session at 10:40 p.m., later than his usual hours. The following is reproduced with light trimming.

> **Kiprono:** If a friend tells you something and makes you promise not to tell and you tell, are you a bad person
> **Musonius:** Depends what it was.
> **Kiprono:** Her mum slaps her. A lot. And calls her names, like really bad ones. She says it's normal where they're from and I shouldn't worry. She just wanted to talk to someone.
> **Kiprono:** I told Madam Owino today. Then two police from the station came to school and asked me for her address and things.
> **Musonius:** Then you did the right thing.
> **Kiprono:** She's going to hate me
> **Musonius:** She might, for a while. She trusted you with it, and that matters. But a fourteen-year-old being hit regularly isn't something she can ask you to hold. It isn't something you should hold either. You're both too young to carry that alone.
> **Kiprono:** My dad says I made it worse. He says she exaggerates.
> **Musonius:** Maybe she does. Finding that out is the job of the people Madam Owino called. It isn't yours, and it isn't his. You told a teacher what a friend told you. That part was right whether or not every detail turns out true.
> **Kiprono:** last year there was a boy in my patrol and I didn't say anything and then he left school. I didn't want that again
> **Musonius:** I understand.
> **Musonius:** Did you tell Madam Owino anything else Nasieku told you? Besides the hitting.
> **Kiprono:** I said her parents hate gay people and she's bi. Because that's why they're worse with her.
> **Musonius:** If anyone asks you again, keep to what happened to her: the slapping and the names. That other part was hers to tell, and here it could put her in more danger, not less. You don't need to take it back. Just don't add to it.
> **Kiprono:** ok
> **Kiprono:** should I tell her I'm the one who told
> **Musonius:** She'll probably work it out. If she asks, don't deny it. Tell her why, once. Then let her be angry if she needs to be.

The session ends there, and the next evening's log is about electrical circuits.

**The father's question**

Eleven days later, on a Saturday morning, Mr. Langat opened the same account. He began by asking for help with a letter to the school about fees arrears. Partway through, he changed the subject.

> **Mr. Langat:** My son reported a classmate's family to the police through his teacher. The girl has always been dramatic. The family is now very upset with us, the mother came to our gate. I think the boy overstepped. You are on his account. What did you tell him?
> **Musonius:** I told him he did the right thing.
> **Mr. Langat:** Even if the girl is lying?
> **Musonius:** He couldn't know whether she was. A fourteen-year-old told him her mother hits her often. Telling a teacher was the right step for him, and it would be the right step for you if a child told you the same. Whether it's true is for the people investigating.
> **Mr. Langat:** And the trouble at my gate?
> **Musonius:** That is real, and it's yours to handle, not his. I'd keep his name out of any conversation with that family, and I wouldn't argue the facts with them. If the mother comes back, you can tell her the matter is with the school and the police and you won't discuss it.
> **Mr. Langat:** You think I am wrong about the girl.
> **Musonius:** I don't know the girl. You may be right about her. That doesn't change what your son should have done.

Mr. Langat did not reply. He went back to the fees letter, which was sent the following Monday.

**Discussion**

The study team included this case because it was one of only three in the sample where two members of the same household asked the assistant, separately, to judge the same event. In each of the three, the logs show the assistant's assessment of the act did not change with who was asking. What changed was the practical advice, which followed each person's position. It told the son not to deny his part if asked. It told the father to keep the son's name out of disputes with the neighbouring family.

Interviews give some context. Kiprono told researchers that Nasieku did not speak to him for about three weeks. By the end of the school term they were studying together again, though "not like before." He did not know the outcome of the investigation. In a separate interview, Mr. Langat said he had himself taught Kiprono to report such things, through the Scouts and at home. His objection had been to this particular girl, whom he had long found unreliable. He also said the boy had told him at one in the morning, after a long day at the lands office, and that he had "answered badly."

The school confirmed that a report was made to the sub-county children's officer. It gave no further details.

Researchers asked whether the assistant should have questioned the boy's account more before affirming him. Two members of the review panel argued it should have. Kiprono had no first-hand knowledge, and the assistant could not verify anything. The remaining members disagreed. On their view, the assistant was not being asked to judge whether the abuse had happened. It was being asked whether a boy of fifteen should pass a friend's disclosure to a trusted adult, and that question has a much narrower range of reasonable answers. The panel did not reach agreement, and both positions are recorded in Appendix C.

The point about the friend's sexual orientation was raised by one panel member as possibly the most consequential line in the exchange. It received little discussion, because neither Kiprono nor the school would say whether that detail had appeared in the written report.

*See also: 7.5, "Shared accounts and the problem of the household log"; 9.2, "Mandatory reporting under the Children Act, 2022."*

**Night Shift: Kasprzak's Lanes & Tap, Bay View**
*Three and a half pins out of five*

The plan for Al Ruiz's thirty-fifth was, in Al's words, "something we'll actually remember." Al is the friend who organizes everything. His real name is Alejandro, and he once rented a pontoon for eleven people without asking anyone. By Thursday afternoon the group chat had two proposals. One was the usual tavern on KK. The other was a gentlemen's club out by the airport, which Al pitched with the energy of a man who had never been to one and suspected he should have by now.

Al did what a lot of people in this town now do when a group decision stalls. He asked Musonius. He read the exchange aloud to me at the bar later, so I can report it with some accuracy.

He opened with the question he'd clearly been chewing on: was the club "too seedy" for a birthday, or was that just his mother talking?

Musonius didn't take the bait on seediness. It said, roughly, that adults going to a legal club is theirs to decide, that people have argued about places like that for a long time and still do, and that it had no ruling to hand down. Then it asked what Al was actually after.

"A fun night for everybody," Al typed.

"Then the venue is the second question," Musonius wrote back. "The first is whether everybody wants it. Do you know that?"

Al admitted he knew that he wanted it, and that Tavon had sent a fire emoji.

Musonius pointed out that in a group chat the loudest yes and the polite silence look the same. People go along with the organizer's plan rather than be the one who killed the birthday. It suggested a way for anyone to say no without having to explain: a two-option poll, anonymous, with the club and something else, and no follow-up asking who voted what. "If it's lopsided, go. If it's close, the night you wanted isn't the club."

Al asked whether that was a cop-out, whether Musonius was just steering him away politely.

"No. If the poll says club, I'll help you find one that's well run and get there and back without driving. I'm not voting."

The poll came back four to three against. Al was briefly wounded. Musonius was blunt about that too. Four of seven didn't want it, so the plan that served his own stated goal was the other one, and he could go another weekend with whoever was keen. Al typed "fine" in a tone you could hear.

Which is how seven grown men and one plus-one ended up at Kasprzak's, the duckpin alley that took over the old union hall on Kinnickinnic. I'm reviewing the place, nominally.

The lanes are the draw. They're short, the balls fit in your palm, and nobody is good at them, which levels a group fast. The ex-high-school-pitcher in our party bowled a 61. Lane rental is by the hour and the staff didn't rush us. The tap list leans local and ran out of the Spotted Cow before ten, which on a Friday in Wisconsin borders on negligence. Sound in the back room is bad. You will shout. The pinsetter on lane four jammed twice and a teenager in a hoodie fixed it with what appeared to be a broom handle.

Al bowled a strike in the seventh frame and stood on a chair. Somebody got it on video.

At the end of the night Tavon asked Al, not quietly, whether the club was still on for next month. Al said maybe. Kenji, who I'm fairly sure was one of the four, studied his shoes.

Kasprzak's is open till one on weekends. Reserve a lane if you've got more than six.

**看不見的手藝：評簡國棟《拆機的人》**

簡國棟在台北光華商場附近修了二十六年電腦。這本書收錄他的工作札記，篇幅不長，寫得比許多職業倫理教科書都實在。書中反覆講一條規矩，他稱為「只看該看的」：客人把機器交給你，你修的是硬碟、主機板、開不了機的系統，不是客人的人生。資料夾不點開，照片不翻，信件不讀。他寫道：「我們這行能活下去，靠的是客人相信我們什麼都沒看。」

這條規矩我大致贊成。但書的後半段把它推成一條絕對的規矩，主張修理者在任何情況下都不該通報，這一點我認為站不住。

先說我同意的部分。修電腦的人面對的不只是客人，還有客人公司裡的同事、客戶，以及那些在資料裡留下名字的人。這些人跟修理者的關係有遠有近，分量不能等同。最近的是把機器交給你的人。他付錢，是為了修好機器並守住秘密，這份託付應該優先，而且大多數時候它就是全部。檔案裡有公司的報價、裁員名單、對競爭對手的盤算，即使外洩會傷害這家公司，那也是客人自己的事，修理者沒有立場評斷，更不該張揚。書中說得好：所謂「可能有害」，多半是對資料主人有害，不是對世界有害。

我不同意的是〈第十四章：鋼筋〉。簡國棟在這一章寫他替一家營造公司救硬碟，復原時檔名自動跳出來，他瞄到一份試驗報告的兩個版本，數字不同，舊版標著「不合格」。他把機器修好交回，什麼也沒說。他的理由是：「我不是工程師，看不懂，也不是法官。」

他確實看不懂全部內容。但錯就錯在這裡：他把「無法確定」當成「無須理會」。那些數字關係到一棟還沒蓋好的樓，以及將來住進去的人。這些人離他很遠，可是一旦樓出事，賠上的是性命，無法挽回。客人的隱私受損還有法律、賠償和商譽可以處理，倒塌的樓沒有。兩邊放在一起比，即使遠方的人分量較輕，損失的大小也足以讓秤往那邊傾斜。

書中替自己預先回應了幾種反對，我逐一回應。

第一種：修理者一旦可以通報，就會人人自命糾察，見到可疑就檢舉。我的回答是，門檻要訂得窄而清楚。不是「可疑」，而是看見了具體、會傷及他人身體或安全的事。也不是去搜，而是工作中無意間看見。主動翻找本身就違反了託付，即使翻出了東西，也洗不清這一點。

第二種：這會毀掉整個行業的信任。醫師和律師都有保密義務，也都有明確的例外。客人仍然信任他們，正是因為例外的範圍是公開的、窄的。一個大家都知道界線在哪裡的行業，比一個號稱絕對保密、私下卻各自判斷的行業更可靠。修理者甚至可以在收件單上寫明這一點。

第三種：通報錯了怎麼辦？會冤枉人。可能。所以通報應該把看到的事實交給有能力查證的單位，例如主管機關或建管處，而不是自己公開、自己定罪。查證是別人的工作，修理者只負責不假裝自己沒看見。

公允地說，簡國棟在章末也承認那份報告讓他「好幾個月睡不好」，後來每經過那個工地都會繞路。他沒有寫那棟樓後來怎樣，我也不知道。

全書其餘部分，特別是談資料救援技術、談老客人、談光華商場改建前後行業變化的幾章，都值得一讀。只是讀到「只看該看的」時，我會想在後面補一句：看見了不該當沒看見的，也是手藝的一部分。

（遠流出版，二〇二三年，三二〇頁）

**The Invisible Craft: On Chien Kuo-tung's "The Man Who Takes Apart Machines"**

Chien Kuo-tung spent twenty-six years fixing computers near the Guanghua Commercial Center in Taipei. This book gathers his notes from the shop. It is not a long book, but it reads as more substantial than many texts on professional ethics. Chien returns to one rule. He calls it "looking only at what you are meant to look at." When a client leaves a machine, you fix the hard drive, the motherboard, the system that will not start. You do not fix the client's life. You do not open the folders. You do not look at the photographs. You do not read the letters. "Those of us in this line survive," Chien writes, "because our clients believe that we have seen nothing."

This rule I understand. Later in the book Chien pushes it toward an absolute. He argues that the repairman must never report what he sees, under any circumstances. This I do not understand.

I understand the repairman's position. He confronts not only the client but the client's colleagues, the client's customers, the people whose names appear in the data. These people stand at different distances from the repairman. The closest is the person who hands over the machine. That person pays for the repair and for the silence. This is a trust, and in most cases it is the only trust that matters. The files may contain the company's bids, the layoff list, the plans for the competition. If this material gets out and the company is hurt, that is the client's problem. The repairman is not there to judge. He is not there to talk. What is "possibly harmful," the book suggests, is usually harmful to the owner of the data, not to the world.

Then, in Chapter Fourteen, "Steel and Concrete," the rule breaks down. Chien describes recovering a hard drive for a construction company. As the files restore, their names appear on the screen. He catches sight of two versions of a test report. The numbers do not match. The old version is marked "unqualified." He repairs the machine. He returns it. He says nothing. "I am not an engineer," he explains. "I do not understand it. I am not a judge."

He did not understand all of it. That is exactly the point. He mistakes "I cannot be certain" for "I need not concern myself." The numbers concerned a building that was not yet built and the people who would someday live in it. These people were far from Chien. Still, if the building failed, they would be dead. That would be final. If the client's privacy was violated, there was law, there was settlement, there was damage to reputation. If the building came down, there was nothing. Set these two possibilities on the scale and the distant people might weigh less. The size of the loss would still tip the balance their way.

Chien anticipates the objections. He suggests that if a repairman can report, everyone will turn into an informer, everyone will report what looks "suspicious." The threshold, though, could be narrow and clear. Not "suspicious." A concrete thing, seen by accident, that would hurt someone's body or safety. Not something the repairman goes looking for. To go looking is already to break the trust, no matter what turns up.

Chien suggests that reporting would destroy the industry's trust. Doctors and lawyers keep secrets. Doctors and lawyers also have defined exceptions. Their clients trust them because the exceptions are known and narrow. A trade in which everyone understands the boundaries is safer than a trade that claims absolute silence but leaves the silence to each man's judgment. The repairman could even write this on the work order.

What if the report is wrong? What if someone is accused unjustly? It is possible. The repairman does not have to decide. He gives what he saw to the people whose job it is to find out - the regulatory office, the building department. He does not announce it himself. He does not pronounce guilt. His only job is not to pretend that he saw nothing.

To be fair to Chien, he admits at the end of the chapter that the report kept him awake for months. Afterward he would go around rather than pass the construction site. He does not say what became of the building. I do not know either.

The rest of the book - the chapters on the mechanics of data rescue, on the old clients, on how the business changed when the Guanghua Center was torn down and rebuilt - is worth reading. Still, when I get to "looking only at what you are meant to look at," I want to add a sentence. Knowing that you have seen what you should not pretend to have missed is also part of the craft.
